body.text: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth yesterday sought to reassure Southeast Asian counterparts on Wednesday of Washington’s commitment to the region, pledging that the superpower would “let our actions speak for themselves.”

Hegseth made the comments in an address to the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) in Cebu, Philippines, where he once again outlined President Donald Trump’s vision of a “more stable, secure, and prosperous Pacific.”

“The approach we’re taking we described as strong, quiet, and clear – strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics,” he said, according to the official transcript of his remarks.

In line with this approach, the U.S. would “let our actions speak for themselves, but clear enough that our friends, our partners, and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners.”

To support that, Hegseth said that the U.S. would back that commitment with practical cooperation, such as “strengthening maritime domain awareness, improving interoperability, and advancing cooperation among our navies.”

“These are not symbolic things. They are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do,” he added. “Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict.”

Hegseth also proposed that the two sides develop a “U.S.-ASEAN Framework for Defense Cooperation to act as a “practical framework” for cooperation in the coming years, although he did not offer any further details of the proposed pact.

Hegseth’s promise of “pragmatism, openness to dialogue, respect for counterparts, and proud nationalism,” a reiteration of the realist theme of his address to the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, in principle aligns well with ASEAN’s own modus operandi. But just how reassuring this would have been to Southeast Asian interlocutors attempting to deal with the volatility and caprice of the second Trump administration remains unclear.

Most Southeast Asian nations, and particularly those with outstanding maritime disputes with China, would likely welcome sustained or enhanced U.S. security cooperation. This is especially important for the Philippines, which has the distinction of being both a U.S. treaty ally and a South China Sea claimant state that disputes China’s maximalist claims to the vital waterway. The past few years have seen growing tensions between Beijing and Manila in contested parts of the South China Sea, where the two sides have engaged in a string of dangerous confrontations.

In his own remarks to the ADMM, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said that ASEAN values the United States’ “sustained engagement” with the region’s defense establishments, pointing out that “a robust U.S. presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific region.”

Even then, the erratic nature of current U.S. foreign policy would likely be a source of consternation in most, if not all, ASEAN capitals. Southeast Asia has been hit hard by the effects of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year, which exposed the heavy dependence of most nations on imported oil and refined fuels from the Gulf. The Trump administration’s erratic tariff policy – Southeast Asian nations were among the heaviest hit by Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff announcement – has also impacted the region’s economies, and prompted some nations to begin diversifying their trade partnerships. On top of this, the U.S.’ staunch support for Israel, and its role in the Israeli assaults on Gaza, remains a subject of concern in Muslim-majority Southeast Asia.

Even in terms of security cooperation and military deployments, a traditional area of strength, the U.S. walks a fine line between supporting deterrence by bolstering Southeast Asian defense capacity and actions that ratchet up tensions with China. While the Trump administration has dialed down tensions with Beijing, its highly disruptive war on Iran, the accompanying rhetoric of which has hardly eschewed “needless escalation or public theatrics,” naturally raises the question of whether this U.S. administration, or a future Trump-ite administration, could bluster its way into some sort of conflict with China.

Greg Poling, director of the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C., told Reuters that Hegseth would get an opportunity to discuss the above issues with ASEAN counterparts, although he expected that concrete cooperation would be concentrated among “like-minded” countries.
